content:
According to reports yesterday, Apple has agreed to comply with the EU's "fairer" App Tracking Transparency (ATT) rules, following an investigation by the German antitrust watchdog.

Apple said the commitment is voluntary, and to our understanding, they will make a total of eight modifications to comply with the requirements...

The personal data collected by developers often far exceeds what the app needs to function. What Apple calls "app tracking" is one example — serving you personalised ads based on the interests reflected by the apps you have installed, whether inside apps or on the web. App Tracking Transparency (ATT) is about giving you a choice over whether this data can be collected and used in this way.

Apple said yesterday that the Federal Cartel Office (FCO) recognises the value of giving users a choice; in fact, the FCO's report stated that they welcome ATT from a data protection perspective, and other domestic privacy regulators have similarly expressed support.

The FCO's objection appears to be that Apple's existing prompt makes "app tracking" sound scarier than it actually is. The iPhone maker will make eight modifications in response, including removing the word "track".

  • Change the colour of the top icon element in the prompt from orange to blue
  • Update the ATT prompt to display full-page
  • Remove the word "track" from the ATT prompt and the "Personalised Ads" prompt
  • Change the ATT choice buttons from "Allow" and "Ask App Not to Track" to "Allow" and "Deny"
  • Allow formatting variations (such as bold, italics, and bulleted lists) to be included in the ATT prompt
  • Add an option for developers to display an additional page of information directly from the prompt to provide further GDPR information. Developers can already do this by showing a custom prompt before the ATT prompt.
  • Allow developers to ask users again with the ATT prompt one year after they have made a decision, regardless of whether their choice at the time was "Allow" or "Deny"
  • Make minor wording adjustments to the "Personalised Ads" prompt to make it clearer, but without changing the effect or meaning of the wording

Apple told us they are committed to ensuring ATT continues to be available in EU countries, and that the measure has been welcomed by privacy advocacy groups, data protection authorities, and iPhone users.

The company reiterated that its own apps do not show the ATT prompt because they do not use personal data collected from apps to serve targeted advertising or measure advertising effectiveness. They stressed that third-party apps are treated exactly the same way — if a third-party app does not collect this data, it does not need to display a prompt.

9to5Mac's take

For all sides, this appears to be the best outcome. iPhone users can still make a choice, but based on a prompt that more accurately reflects the decision they need to make — namely, between personalised ads and not having personalised ads.

This investigation also addresses external concerns about Apple's own advertising sales business. The company has made clear that they do not use data collected from their own apps to serve personalised ads, nor to measure advertising effectiveness.
